title: Sense and Sensibility
author: Jane Austen
openingText: The family of Dashwood had long been settled in Sussex. Their estate was large, and their residence was at Norland Park, in the centre of their property, where, for many generations, they had lived in so respectable a manner as to engage the general good opinion of their surrounding acquaintance. The late owner of this estate was a single man, who lived to a very advanced age, and who for many years of his life, had a constant companion and housekeeper in his sister. But her death, which happened ten years before his own, produced a great alteration in his home; for to supply her loss, he invited and received into his house the family of his nephew Mr. Henry Dashwood, the legal inheritor of the Norland estate, and the person to whom he intended to bequeath it. In the society of his nephew and niece, and their children, the old Gentleman’s days were comfortably spent. His attachment to them all increased. The constant attention of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Dashwood to his wishes, which proceeded not merely from interest, but from goodness of heart, gave him every degree of solid comfort which his age could receive; and the cheerfulness of the children added a relish to his existence.
about:
When Henry Dashwood dies, his widow and three daughters lose the security of Norland, their family home. The property passes to his son by an earlier marriage. A promise of financial help is steadily reasoned away, and the women begin again in a cottage in Devonshire. There, Elinor and Marianne encounter new neighbours, new attachments, and new reasons to question what another person's behaviour can tell them.

Elinor feels deeply but guards what she reveals. Marianne regards unreserved feeling as a test of sincerity. Austen gives neither sister a simple monopoly on wisdom: restraint can conceal suffering, while emotional openness can mistake conviction for knowledge. Visits, music, letters, and apparently trivial conversations become tests of loyalty and judgment.

Published in 1811, the novel makes courtship inseparable from income, inheritance, family obligation, and reputation. Its comedy is often sharpest when a character finds a perfectly respectable explanation for doing exactly what suits them. Read for the distance between what people say, what they know, and what their actions cost somebody else.

whyItMatters.title: A promise can disappear one reasonable step at a time
whyItMatters.body:
John and Fanny Dashwood turn a dying father's request into an argument for giving almost nothing. The comedy depends on watching self-interest borrow the language of prudence and care.

Today: Notice how a convenient explanation can make a broken promise feel responsible.

whyItMatters.title: Feeling and showing are different things
whyItMatters.body:
Elinor's restraint and Marianne's openness invite different judgments from the people around them. Austen asks how much we can know of suffering from its outward performance, and who carries the burden when others assume that composure means ease.

Today: A calm person may still need support.

whyItMatters.title: Romantic freedom has material conditions
whyItMatters.body:
The Dashwood women must weigh affection within a world of inherited wealth, limited incomes, and dependence on relatives. A house, a carriage, or an invitation can change what appears possible in a relationship.

Today: Ask how money and housing shape the choices that seem purely personal.

angleCards.title: Follow the money
angleCards.text: Track the sums, gifts, houses, and expectations surrounding each courtship. Who controls the resources, and whose future depends on their goodwill?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow how inheritance, income, and gifts shape choices in Sense and Sensibility, without reducing every attachment to a financial bargain.

angleCards.title: Read the silences
angleCards.text: Watch what Elinor does not say and how other people interpret it. Compare private knowledge with the feelings a conversation allows her to show.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the costs and uses of Elinor’s restraint, especially when her silence is mistaken for a lack of feeling.

angleCards.title: Test romantic certainty
angleCards.text: Marianne trusts shared tastes and strong emotions. Notice when the evidence supports her confidence and when a compelling story takes the place of evidence.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow how Marianne forms her judgments and ask when emotional sincerity helps or obstructs her understanding of others.

angleCards.title: Listen for the excuse
angleCards.text: Attend to speeches that turn advantage into duty or selfishness into good sense. Ask where the narrator lets a character condemn themselves without an explicit verdict.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Austen’s irony through the gap between a character’s respectable explanation and the consequences of their behaviour.

cast.name: Elinor Dashwood
cast.description: Nineteen, perceptive, affectionate, and careful in judgment. She manages practical difficulties while trying to keep her own feelings from governing everyone else’s life.

cast.name: Marianne Dashwood
cast.description: Not yet seventeen at the opening, musical and passionately responsive to books, landscapes, and people. She distrusts restraint when she believes there is nothing shameful to hide.

cast.name: Mrs. Dashwood
cast.description: Henry Dashwood’s widow. Generous, impulsive, and deeply attached to her children, she shares Marianne’s readiness to hope and feel without moderation.

cast.name: Margaret Dashwood
cast.description: Thirteen at the opening, good-natured and influenced by Marianne’s romantic outlook. She notices more of her sisters’ affairs than they always wish her to report.

cast.name: John Dashwood
cast.description: Henry’s son by his first marriage and the new owner of Norland. Respectable conduct and an accommodating conscience allow him to think well of his generosity.

cast.name: Fanny Dashwood
cast.description: Born a Ferrars, she guards her household’s money and prospects closely. Her advice to John gives family duty an increasingly economical interpretation.

cast.name: Edward Ferrars
cast.description: Quiet and shy, with more interest in a comfortable private life than the public distinction his family wants for him. Elinor values qualities that are not immediately striking.

cast.name: Sir John Middleton
cast.description: A sociable landowner who offers the Dashwoods Barton Cottage. His genuine kindness comes with an inexhaustible enthusiasm for visits and parties.

cast.name: Mrs. Jennings
cast.description: A cheerful widow with a comfortable income and two married daughters. She turns her attention to everyone else’s marriages, often with embarrassing jokes.

cast.name: Colonel Brandon
cast.description: A reserved, gentlemanly man in his mid-thirties. His attentive quietness contrasts with the noise of the Barton circle.

cast.name: John Willoughby
cast.description: A handsome young man whose energy and enthusiasm for music and books appeal to Marianne. He enters the Dashwoods’ circle through an unexpected act of assistance.
